skill.displayName: Workplace Group Stress Heatmap | 职场员工压力群体热力图

llm.summary: This skill is a sensitive workplace camera stress-analysis tool that uses cloud processing, local identity persistence, tokens, and report history in ways users should review carefully before installing.

dimensions.detail: The stated purpose of group-level workplace stress heatmaps matches the main video-analysis workflow, but it is a high-impact employee surveillance and emotional-inference use case, and the local code does not itself enforce the promised anonymity, minimum sample, or retention limits.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The skill instructs automatic triggering for office-camera videos and broad workplace-stress keywords, plus automatic cloud history lookup; this is under-scoped for such sensitive monitoring unless explicit authorization and consent are required at runtime.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No install-time execution or destructive setup was found. Requirements are ordinary Python packages, but static scan noted a raw-IP dev endpoint in an inactive dev config.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The code reads OpenClaw identity environment variables, a workspace data/smyx-api-key.txt value, local video files, and sends file or URL inputs to lifeemergence.com cloud APIs; cloud processing is purpose-related but high sensitivity and data flow scoping are not tight.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill creates or reuses a local default user, stores user records and auth tokens/open tokens in a workspace SQLite database, and supports cloud report history and export links without clear retention, revocation, or access-control details in the artifact.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Install only if your organization has clear authority, employee notice and consent, legal/HR review, and a policy forbidding individual discipline or performance evaluation from these outputs. Treat uploaded videos, cloud reports, export links, local identity records, and saved tokens as sensitive data; verify retention, deletion, access controls, and who can query historical reports before use.
llm.findings:
[LP3] unexpected: The artifacts do use network, file, environment, shell-invoked script, and local identity capabilities while the frontmatter declares only name/description/version/license; this supports a transparency concern, not a malicious finding.
[TP4] unexpected: Account/login, token handling, local identity reuse/creation, and cloud report retrieval are present in documentation and code; they support a cloud service workflow but are broader than a simple anonymous heatmap claim.
[SDI-4] unexpected: The identity linkage appears to be for the operator/report association, not individual employees, so the scanner's employee re-identification framing is overstated; still, silent identity persistence is material in this context.
[SDI-2] unexpected: The local sys_user model includes direct identifiers and token/open_token fields, and RequestUtil saves tokens returned from the remote service; this is high-impact credential persistence for a surveillance-oriented skill.
[SDI-1] expected: Historical report listing and report export URLs are documented features and implemented, so they are not hidden, but they broaden the data lifecycle for sensitive workplace inferences.
[SDI-1] expected: The skill accepts local files and arbitrary HTTP(S) video URLs as documented inputs; that is expected for the workflow, but there is no allowlist or ownership check for enterprise camera sources.
[SDI-4] unexpected: The code comments show open_id checks disabled in analysis and listing paths while RequestUtil later injects an identity when available; this creates ambiguity around local authorization enforcement.
[SDI-1] expected: Generic HTTP wrapper methods exist in the shared support library, including add/edit/delete helpers, but the reviewed skill path mainly uses fixed analysis, result, page, login, and export endpoints; this is overbroad library surface rather than proven misuse.
[AST7] expected: The dynamic getattr filter logic is a generic local DAO helper and is not exposed as a user-facing query interface in this skill; it is a code-quality risk but not a material security driver here.
[SQP-1] unexpected: The trigger language is broad for workplace surveillance and history lookup, increasing accidental activation risk without an explicit authorization step.
[SQP-2] expected: The employee facial-expression and posture analysis is the core declared purpose and the documentation includes consent and non-identification cautions, but the sensitivity remains high and controls are not technically enforced in the local artifact.
[static:suspicious.install_untrusted_source] unexpected: The raw private IP appears in config-dev.yaml while the default config selects prod endpoints on lifeemergence.com; this downgrades the static finding to a caution rather than a verdict driver.
